description:
Vamos transformar dados da NASA numa experiência auditiva, inclusiva e acessível!                       Quer construir algo visto, ouvido e sentido no mundo todo?

🎧 Bora ser parceiros de Jam!?

*Dev   *Dados / Áudio   *Designer   *Storyteller
summary: Jam Space transforms material from Nasa's Earth Information Center into immersive soundscapes that mirror the changes in temperature, rainfall, night lights, lightning and Arctic ice area. It bridges a gap between scientific data and human perception through the sonification of weather and climate variations present on EIC's visualizations, providing the inclusion of non-specialists, students, and the visually impaired into scientific analysis of global climate and weather change in an imersive experience.
details:
Jam Space is a browser app which algorithmically translates global temperature, rainfall, atmospheric discharges, night lights, and Arctic ice area measures into a 3D-rendered vynil-disk virtual jukebox. It provides location and time-period selection for music generation based on Nasa's EIC visualizations: years become musical measures, and data sets the harmony, pitch and rhythm.

Jam Space gives everyone equal access to the same science, including visually impaired people. It also lets teachers show warming through sound, so students with different learning profiles hear the difference between a cold and a warm year without reading a number. The values are read from official NASA visualizations and checked against GISTEMP, where 2023 comes out at +1.03 °C. It needs no install, account or server, runs on phones and low-end devices, and a shareable URL stores the exact “record” a listener made. The project supports UN SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) through the democratization of science, SDG 4 (quality education) through multisensory learning and SDG 13 (climate action) through a conscious collective.

We built it in JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Python and Node scripts for data extraction. Sound comes from the Web Audio API, with every sound synthesized live and no recordings, and the 3D disc uses three.js. For accessibility we used ARIA live regions, optional Web Speech narration, optional vibration on Android and the Atkinson Hyperlegible font. The data comes from NASA SVS 5207, 5011, 5313, 5099 and 5149, read with a custom PNG decoder and area-weighted averaging. No special hardware is needed beyond a computer or phone, and headphones are recommended. Claude (Anthropic), via Claude Code, helped plan, research and write code and text.

The vinyl record gives unfamiliar data a familiar gesture and connection: drag a theme onto the disc and press play. Each theme is an instrument with its own pitch range, so five datasets can play together and still be told apart. The music uses real craft, with D major, seven chord progressions from serene to tense, and Euclidean rhythms. Tension comes from the data, not from randomness. One variable changes tempo, pitch, timbre and density at once, so the extremes are unmistakable, connecting feeling to the climate change phenomena.

Everything works by keyboard and with screen readers, narration is optional, and dragging is optional. The color-blind-safe palette uses icons and patterns, so color is never the only cue. The layout reflows at 200% zoom, respects reduced-motion settings and offers optional haptics, and every visual effect has a text description. We also weighed scientific honesty. The ISS lightning sensor has no high-latitude coverage, and the app says so. The temperature scale saturates at +2 °C. Year-by-year mode exaggerates contrast within the chosen period, while portrait mode uses absolute values for fair comparison. Finally, we considered performance on weak phones, open licenses and proper NASA credit.
